messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas, a 32-year-old European-American man, has been struggling with intense anxiety and fear since his traumatic experience of being stalked over several months. The stalking culminated in an incident where Thomas was followed to his home by someone he suspected was the stalker. During this time, the individual would send threatening messages and make calls late at night, often expressing anger that seemed directed specifically at him. This experience has left Thomas with a heightened sense of threat and pervasive distrust. Thomas’s triggers are deeply embedded in his daily life. The sound of motorcycle noise, for instance, instantly brings back memories of when he heard the stalker’s motorcycle approaching while he was walking home late one night. He recalls feeling petrified as the bike followed him closely, its engine roaring ominously in the darkness. Even now, any motorbike passing by on the street can cause his heart to race and his palms to sweat. Another trigger is other people expressing anger, even calmly. Thomas vividly remembers a time when he was at home alone, and the stalker had called, their voice dripping with rage. That experience has made him hyper-aware of any signs of anger from others. Recently, while teaching a class, a student raised his voice in frustration over a difficult concept, and Thomas found himself immediately feeling on edge, unable to concentrate or maintain composure. Feeling followed or tracked is another potent trigger for Thomas. He recalls walking home one night when he saw someone watching him from across the street. His heart pounded as he quickened his pace, but the figure stayed in view. This experience has left him constantly vigilant and wary of anyone who seems to be observing him. Recently, while taking a walk with his wife in a familiar park near their house, Thomas felt unnerved by someone walking behind them. He couldn’t shake off the feeling that he was being followed again. Thomas’s coping mechanisms have also shifted significantly since the stalking incident. He often tells himself that he deserves to suffer for what happened, believing that there must be something inherently wrong with him to attract such a stalker. This self-punishing thought has made it difficult for Thomas to seek help or even enjoy his hobbies and interests. His relationship with his wife has also been affected by these maladaptive strategies. Thomas avoids being emotionally close or intimate with her, fearing that he might bring the same danger into their lives again. He struggles to relax because it feels dangerous; instead of enjoying moments of peace, he often finds himself on high alert, scanning for any signs of threat. Thomas’s avoidance behaviors have extended to his daily life and work as a tutor. He avoids going to unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger. For instance, he recently declined an invitation from colleagues to visit a new coffee shop down the street, citing that it was too risky to go somewhere unknown. This behavior has led him to isolate himself further, impacting both his professional and personal life. Sleep problems have also become increasingly severe for Thomas. He often lies awake at night, mind racing with thoughts of being stalked again. His wife has noticed his difficulty in falling asleep and staying asleep, which has added to the strain on their relationship. Thomas experiences frequent false alarms, reacting as if he is in danger even when nothing is actually wrong. A sudden noise outside or an unexpected shadow in a dimly lit room can trigger intense fear responses. He admits that this heightened sense of threat has made it difficult for him to engage fully with his surroundings. The negative appraisals have deeply influenced Thomas’s outlook on life. He struggles with self-doubt, constantly questioning whether he will do the right thing and if he is capable of making sound decisions. This mistrust extends to others as well; he believes that people are not what they seem, and that they cannot be trusted. These beliefs have made it difficult for Thomas to form close relationships or even trust his own judgment. What finally brought Thomas to seek help was the realization that these fears were increasingly isolating him from those around him. He feared losing his wife and the life he had built due to his constant state of hypervigilance and avoidance. While he is scared about what might happen if he confronts these fears, he is most hopeful for a sense of safety and trust again in his daily life.
